title: An f32 as an exact C literal
starter:
(* x is already an f32 value (held in an OCaml float). Return C source that
   produces exactly x:  NAN for any nan, INFINITY, (-INFINITY), and otherwise
   the hex float that Printf's %h prints, with an f suffix: 1.0 -> "0x1p+0f". *)
let c_float (x : float) : string =
  Printf.sprintf "%gf" x
hints: Handle the three special values first: `Float.is_nan`, `infinity` and `neg_infinity`. Everything else is an ordinary finite number.
`Printf.sprintf "%h" x` prints the exact bits as a hex float, like `0x1.99999ap-4`. C reads that same syntax; it just needs the `f` suffix to be a `float` instead of a `double`.

Why `(-INFINITY)` with parentheses: the literal lands inside bigger C expressions, and a leading minus can merge with an operator printed just before it (`x--INFINITY` lexes as `x-- INFINITY`). The same risk applies to negative finite literals if you print them right after an operator, so parenthesize those too in your renderer, or always put spaces around operators.
explain: A hex float names the exact binary value, so it can't be misread the way a short decimal can (`%g` turns FLT_MAX into 3.40282e+38, which reads back as a different float). The solution special-cases nan (with either sign) and the infinities, which have no numeric literal, and prints everything else with `%h` plus `f`, including -0.0 as `-0x0p+0f`.
